extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (learners of proof techniques) / readers of an introductory proofs text
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exercises on proving statements by mathematical induction and using recursion: how to set up base cases, form inductive hypotheses, perform the induction step (including proof by cases), use induction on sizes of finite sets, guess formulas from initial terms, and convert/verify recursive definitions to closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of an induction proof (base case and induction step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove P(0) (or the appropriate base n) and then prove that for any natural number n, if P(n) is true then P(n+1) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The base case need not be n=0; choose the base appropriate to the problem (e.g., n≥1). In the induction step let n be arbitrary and assume P(n) (inductive hypothesis) to prove P(n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce size parameter when statement doesn't mention naturals
rubrics_metrics.description: When a goal does not explicitly mention natural numbers, rephrase it by introducing n as 'B has n elements' (or similar) so you can apply induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove every finite nonempty subset B ⊆ A has a minimal element, restate as ∀n ≥ 1 ∀B ⊆ A(B has n elements → B has a minimal element) and use induction on n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scratch work to guess formulas from small n
rubrics_metrics.description: To conjecture a closed-form formula for a recursively-defined sequence or summation, compute the first several values and look for a pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compute a0,a1,a2,... to guess an = 2^n − 1 before proving by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate n+1 case to n case algebraically
rubrics_metrics.description: In the induction step, express the object for n+1 in terms of the n-case (e.g., use recursive definitions like an+1 = an·a or (n+1)! = (n+1)·n!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the recursive definition or algebraic manipulation to reduce P(n+1) to a statement involving P(n); for divisibility proofs relate an+1 − bn+1 to an − bn (e.g., an+1 − bn+1 = a(an − bn) + ?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an element to remove to produce the smaller instance
rubrics_metrics.description: When inducting on finite sets or structures, remove one element to produce a substructure with n elements and apply the inductive hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prove every finite nonempty B has a minimal element by removing arbitrary b ∈ B and applying the hypothesis to B\{b}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by cases inside an induction step when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the truth of P(n+1) depends on a binary relation or comparison, split into cases (e.g., b R c or ¬b R c) and handle each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case may use contradiction and the inductive hypothesis; choose cases guided by available comparisons in the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential goals: construct or choose witness using inductive hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the goal is existential (∃x ...), use the inductive hypothesis to obtain a witness for the smaller instance and extend or modify it to produce a witness for the larger instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a variable to stand for the witness guaranteed by the inductive hypothesis and reason about it (e.g., choose c minimal in B\{b}).

rubrics_metrics.name: When direct induction fails, try proving a stronger statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes P(n) → P(n+1) is hard; replace P(n) with a stronger property Q(n) such that Q(n) implies P(n) and Q(n) is easier to prove inductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show (1+x)^n > nx, prove the stronger (1+x)^n ≥ 1 + nx so the induction step works cleanly (use nx^2 ≥ 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Base case selection and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the statement for the smallest n of interest (may be n=0, n=1, or another m); correct base ensures induction reaches all desired n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check arithmetic/combinatorial base cases explicitly (e.g., n=3 polygon angular sum, n=1 tiling case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recursive definitions to define functions or sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Define functions/sums by giving base value(s) and a rule for computing f(n+1) from f(n); this both defines the object and suggests induction proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example recursive definitions: f(0)=1, f(n+1)=(n+1)·f(n) (factorial); f(0)=1, f(n+1)=f(n)+2^{n+1} (sum of powers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting recursive definitions to closed forms via induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Guess a closed-form using initial terms and prove by induction that the closed-form satisfies the same recurrence and base case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prove an = 2^n − 1 satisfies a0=0 and an+1 = 2an+1, or show sum formulas by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide-and-conquer tiling / combinatorial inductive strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Split a large combinatorial/geometric instance into smaller subinstances of the same type, place a small gadget to make subinstances exactly the inductive hypothesis's form, then apply inductive hypothesis to each subinstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tile a 2^{n+1}×2^{n+1} board with one square removed by splitting into four 2^n×2^n boards and placing one central L-tromino to make each subboard have one square removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structure-specific properties in the induction (e.g., partial orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit domain-specific facts (transitivity, antisymmetry, minimal elements) together with inductive construction choices (choose R-minimal element) to ensure extension/compatibility in the inductive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: extend a partial order to a total order by removing an R-minimal element and applying induction to remaining set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for common induction fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid incorrectly concluding 'since n was arbitrary, every natural number has property P' within the induction step; do not assume what you need to prove without using the inductive mechanism properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of bad proofs are discussed: e.g., claiming A=N because 0∈A and 'if n∈A then n+1∈A' without proper structure of induction, or misuse of arbitrariness inside induction step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic inequalities and nonnegativity to complete induction inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving inequalities, multiply or expand using the inductive hypothesis and bound nonnegative terms (e.g., nx^2 ≥ 0) to reach desired comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction on more than one parameter or treating some parameters as fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: When statement involves multiple quantifiers (e.g., for all real a and all natural m,n), fix some parameters (treat as arbitrary constants) and induct on one parameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prove am+n = am·an by fixing a and m and using induction on n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive notation / summation as a basis for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use summation notation and define sums recursively (base n=m, recurrence adding a_{n+1}) to justify induction proofs on summations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide base case n=m and recurrence n+1: sum_{i=m}^{n+1} a_i = sum_{i=m}^n a_i + a_{n+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hints and small-step guidance are legitimate parts of an inductive solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small algebraic manipulations, suggested hints in problem statements, and intermediate equations to guide how to connect an+1 with an (or other analogous transitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow explicit hints (e.g., in divisibility problems, complete the equation an+1 − bn+1 = a(an − bn) + ?) and try plugging in small values to adjust guessed formulas.
